ABSTRACT To achieve the balance on economy and ecology, it is indispensable to explore the greener and more inexpensive method for the production of cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs). Herein, a deep eutectic solvent (DES) system based on choline chloride (ChCl) and ethylene glycol (EG) was employed as the swollen solvent, combining with screw extrusion and permeant, to fabricate unmodified CNFs with high yield and thermal stability. The proposed method in this work was simple, convenient, and industrially viable.

The hydrous DESs were applied in the process of CNFs preparation and dispersion to reduce the cost and viscosity of DES. To reveal the principle of CNFs preparation, the impact of sulfuric acid and water content of DES system on the chemical, physical, morphological, thermal, and dispersive properties of CNFs was systematically studied. Properties of the dispersed solvents were characterized by solvatochromic parameters and viscosity parameters to evaluate the potential influence on the preparation and dispersion of CNFs. In general, this work would play valuable guidance in realizing the preparation and dispersion of CNFs via a versatile DES solvent system, thus endowing cellulose materials high-value utilization.

# 1. Introduction Cellulose, as an inexhaustible and widespread natural and green polymer (annual production capacity was around 75-100 billion tons worldwide), had attracted wide of increasing concern because of the global warming and depletion of petroleum sources [1,2]. Cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs), a kind of renewable and biodegradable cellulose nanomaterials [3,4], had received much attention in recent years because of the excellent features such as high strength and stiffness, high specific surface area, low density, biodegradability, and renewability. These advantages suggested that CNFs had great potential application prospect in composites to replace plastics [5,6], gel materials [7,8], catalysis [9,10], adsorption [11,12], electronics [13,14], and biomedical systems [15]. However, the structural complexity of components in natural cell walls limited the productivity of CNFs. Therefore, more
efforts should be devoted to developing a highly efficient and eco-friendly method for CNFs preparation, which was conducive to reap the full potential value of cellulose nanomaterials in the future.

Cellulose fibrils contained crystalline and amorphous regions and it could be delaminated to CNFs via mechanical and mechanochemical methods. It was well known that the structure of cellulose fibrils was complex and tightly-packed formed by hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces. Therefore, the mechanical treatment could defibrillate the fibers and transformed to CNFs as the mechanical energy exceeded the interfibrillar bond energy. Common methods for mechanical production of CNFs included high-pressure homogenization [16], ball milling [12], grinding [17] and so on.

Scientists gradually recognized the problem and have found some new approaches to compensate for the shortcomings of single mechanical treatment for CNFs preparation. Chemical or biological pretreatment could swell cellulose fibers and partially disrupt the hydrogen bond network of cellulose fibrils, thus increasing the accessibility of cellulose fibrils [19]. That is, compared to single mechanical treatment, combining biochemical pretreatments with mechanical action could be conducive to reduce the energy consumption and improve the efficiency of fibrillation during the process of CNFs preparation. Thus far, various kinds of biochemical pretreatments have been used in CNFs preparation, such as acid hydrolysis, oxidation reaction, enzymatic hydrolysis, and so on. In the pretreatment of acid hydrolysis, the representative species mainly contained mineral acids (like sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, and phosphoric acid) and organic acids (like p-toluenesulfonic acid, oxalic acid, and maleic acid). It was well known that the acid hydrolysis could remove the amorphous of cellulose and partially disrupt the hydrogen bond network of cellulose fibrils, thus benefiting the liberation of CNFs via various mechanical treatments [20]. Oxidation reaction of cellulose mainly consisted of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl radical (TEMPO)-mediated oxidation and periodate-chlorite oxidation. Oxidation reaction could selectively oxidize the primary hydroxyl groups to weaken inter-fibrillar hydrogen bonds of cellulose, which would facilitate the extraction of CNFs [21]. However, the main obstacles during the process of CNFs preparation such as the harsh chemical consumption, corrosion of the equipment, and impacting environment still existed. The principle of enzymatic pretreatment on cellulose was similar to acid hydrolysis. However, enzymatic pretreatment was milder and more eco-friendly compared with acid hydrolysis or oxidation reaction [22]. Unfortunately, there were still some drawbacks in enzymatic pretreatment such as long reaction time, high operation cost, and so on. Therefore, to achieve the balance on economy and ecology, it is indispensable to explore a greener, simpler, and more inexpensive method for the pretreatment of cellulose.

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), as new green solvents with biode- gradability and eco-friendly nature, were simply synthesized by mixing hydrogen-bond donors (HBD, such as quaternary ammonium salts) with hydrogen-bond acceptors (HBA, such as amines, amides, carboxylic

acids, polyol) [23]. This meant that the properties of DESs could be flexibly designable through adjusting the HBA and HBD types and molar ratios to meet practical application needs. Apart from the above, DESS possessed many distinct physicochemical properties similar to ionic liquids, such as low melting points, negligible vapor pressure, high thermal stability, and nonflammability [24]. It was known that ionic liquids were recognized as good solvents for treatment of cellulose [25]. Thus, more and more researches employed DESs as the swollen solvents to pretreat the biomass to produce CNFs. Liu et al. applied an acidic DES based on choline chloride and citric acid in the pretreatment of bleached softwood kraft pulp and combined with high-pressure homogenize to prepare CNFs [26]. Hong et al. selected the DES composed of choline chloride and oxalic acid to swell the luffa sponge and adopted a two-step ultrasonication treatment to prepare elongated CNFs [27]. Unfortu- nately, DESs employed as swollen solvents in the process of CNFs preparation were commonly acidic DESs in most researches, which would cause the side reactions like esterification between acidic DESS and CNFs. More than this, it was known that high viscosity of DESs was a key problem, which would cause mass transfer problems and low dissolution mass concentration [28]. High cost of DESs was another key concern hindering the widespread application of DESs. Adding water to the DES system was recognized as a simple, efficient and low-cost method to tailor the properties of DESs, which could reduce the vis- cosity and cost of DESS [29]. To our knowledge, there were still few studies on the hydrated natural DESs applied in the preparation and dispersion of unmodified CNFs remained among the gaps.

Herein, we aimed to use a natural DES as the swollen solvent fol- lowed by extrusion and permeation to prepare unmodified CNFs with high yield and thermal stability. The proposed method in this work was simple, convenient, and industrially viable. Moreover, to reduce the cost and viscosity of DES, the hydrous DESs were innovatively applied in the process of CNFs preparation and dispersion. Ethylene glycol (EG) was recognized as one of common biomass-derived polyols and showed a high boiling point and fascinating compatibility with biomass. In this work, EG was employed as HBD and choline chloride as HBA to syn- thesize the natural DES, which was used as a well-swollen solvent to pretreat cellulose under high temperature. Then, the swollen cellulose fibers were crushed and permeated using a screw extrusion device. After

## 2. Material and methods ### 2.1. Materials The Needle Bleached Kraft Pulp (NBKP) was provided from Jiangsu Province of China. Sulfuric acid (H2SO4, 98%), Ethylene glycol (C2H6O2, 98%), Choline chloride (C5H14ClNO, 98%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Bio-Chem Technology Co. Ltd., China. Cupri- ethylenediamine solution (C2H18N4O2Cu) was purchased from China National Pulp and Paper Research Institute. All chemicals were used as received without any purification.

## 2.2. Methods The uniform and clear DES was synthesized by ChCl and EG at a molar of 1:1 under 100 °C for 1 h. Four hydrated DESs were obtained by mixing the DES with water at the mass ratio of 80:20, 60:40, 40:60, and 20:80, which were referred to as 80% DES, 60% DES, 40% DES, and 20% DES, respectively. The NBKP of oven-dry weight was torn into small pieces and pretreated by DES at a mass ratio of 1:8 (120 °C, 120 min) with mechanical stirring for sufficiently swelling. After this procedure, the crushed cellulose (CC) was obtained using a screw extrusion device (CZR-2014, Guangzhou Chunziran Co. Ltd., China) 3 cycles under 100 °C. The type of screw extrusion was a single screw with L/D ratio of 20 and rotate speed of 55 rpm. 0%, 0.2%, 0.4%, 0.6%, and 0.8% w/w H2SO4 (based on the CC dispersion system) as a catalyst was separately dripped into the CC dispersion system, which was diluted to 5% solid content. The CC dispersion system was fully swelled at 100 °C for 0.5 h to insure that H2SO4 was permeated into the CC dispersion system. The obtained samples with the optimized H2SO4 amount were directly diluted to 0.8% concentration using DES, 80% DES, 60% DES, 40% DES, 20% DES, and distilled water (DW), respectively. Then the diluted samples were refined at 6000 rpm for 40 min under ambient temperature using a colloid mill with the narrow gap between the rotor and the stator was 0.1–3.0 mm (JIM-150, Wenzhou Kangding Machinery co. Ltd., China). Finally, before freeze-drying for later evaluation, the obtained different CNFs samples were dialyzed in DW for 7 days to completely remove DES. The obtained different CNFs samples were named as DES-CNF, 20% DES-CNF, 40% DES-CNF, 60% DES-CNF, 80% DES-CNF, and DW-CNF, respectively.

The viscosity of DES and hydrated DESs were tested using a digital viscosimeter (FANGRUI, NDJ-001, China). All samples were measured by three replicates and the averages were reported.

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. CNFs preparation The flowchart of CNFs preparation was schematically shown in Fig. 1. DESs, as emerging kinds of solvents synthesized by HBA and HBD, were much significant for the swelling of cellulose [34]. It was found that EG exhibited good compatibility with cellulose according to the previous literature [35].

Moreover, EG was one of the biomass-derived polyols and it possessed a high boiling point. Therefore, DES consisted of ChCl and EG could promote cellulose fibrillation under high temperature, due to the strong interaction with cellulose chains. Based on these findings and previous studies by our group [36,37], DES consisted of ChCl and EG was chosen as a swollen solvent to pretreat cellulose and yielded CNFs in this work. Completely DES permeation and swelling of cellulose fibers was not only in favor of increasing the reactive activity but also conducive to the subsequent extrusion process. Second, the fully softened, permeated, and swollen cellulose was crushed using the screw extruder, which combined kneading and feeding screws. Due to the severe mechanical shear force and interaction friction, the fully swollen cellulose fibers were disrupted, torn, and then cut off to finer fibers. It was proved that the cell wall of cellulose fibers could be disintegrated into elementary fibrils during the screw extrusion [39]. Namely, more DES could be absorbed by crushed cellulose fibers under the action of mechanical extrusion. Trigui et al. reported that the swollen cellulose fibers could be successfully disintegrated into CNFs by twin-screw extrusion [40]. Due to the catalysis of H2SO4, cellulose fibrils were more accessible to hydrolyze and the cleavage of linkages among cellulose fibrils was partly broken. The obtained CC dispersion systems with the optimized H2SO4 amount were diluted to 0.8% concentration using DES, 80% DES, 60% DES, 40% DES, 20% DES, and distilled water (DW), respectively, for evaluation of the water content of DES system affecting the preparation and dispersion of CNFs. Ultimately, all samples were delivered into a colloid mill for further refining to prepare CNFs suspensions and the diameters of obtained CNFs were all less than 100 nm (Fig. 1). This phenomenon suggested that CNFs were successfully prepared under the synergism of DES swelling, screw extrusion, a small amount of sulfuric acid catalysis, and mechanical milling.

The DPv of NBKP was 1260 and the control sample (without the addition of H2SO4) was 890, which indicated that DES swelling and mechanical action could effectively reduce the DPv of cellulose [41,42]. When the H2SO4 amount increased from 0.2% to 0.8%, the DPv of samples was decreased from 460 to 255. These results indicated that a small amount of H2SO4 could slightly hydrolyze cellulose fibrils, which played a significant role in the prep- aration of CNFs.

XRD diffraction patterns of obtained CNFs and NBKP were shown in Fig. 4. It was obviously indicated that the crystalline structure of NBKP and all CNFs samples were the cellulose I structure, as the XRD curves of obtained CNFs and NBKP were similar to previous literatures [43]. Thus, we could conclude that the crystal structure of obtained CNFs was hardly changed by DES swelling, mechanical treatment, and H2SO4 catalysis. The degrees of crystallinity computed from the 2θ peaks for the raw material and CNFs using different amounts of H2SO4 catalysis were 75.6%, 63.7%, 74.9%, 76.1%, 77.3%, and 77.6%, respectively. The crystalline index of CNFs without H2SO4 catalysis was the lowest among all samples. It was probably due to the mechanical action, which could destruct the crystalline structure of samples, thus reducing the crystal-line index [17]. When H2SO4 catalysis was employed, the crystalline index of CNFs increased compared with the raw material. Moreover, it could be found that the crystalline index of CNFs became larger as the usage of H2SO4 increased. Combining with the results in our previous studies [36,37], the phenomenon were likely caused by more dissolution of the amorphous region under the action of acid hydrolysis.

## 4. Conclusions High-yield and thermostable CNFs were successfully prepared via DES based on ChCl: EG swelling, screw extrusion and permeant, a minimum supply of sulfuric acid catalysis and colloidal milling, while preserving the natural chemical structure of CNFs. The hydrous DESs were innovatively applied in the process of CNFs preparation and dispersion to reduce the cost and viscosity of DES. To reveal the principle of CNFs preparation and dispersion, the impact of sulfuric acid and water content on the chemical, physical, morphological, thermal, and dispersive properties of CNFs was systematically studied. It was found that the properties of solvents (such as viscosity, solvatochromic properties) had a relationship with the preparation and dispersion of CNFs. More strikingly, the light transmittance of DES-CNF suspension was up to 72.2% and it could remain stable standing for 30 days, showing favorable dispersion and stability. In conclusion, this work, which was simple and industrially viable, would play valuable guidance on realizing the preparation and dispersion of CNFs via a versatile DES solvent system, thus making cellulose materials high-value utilization.

Cellulose nanofibrils Deep eutectic solvent Screw extrusion Solvent properties High yield Thermal stability ABSTRACT To achieve the balance on economy and ecology, it is indispensable to explore the greener and more inexpensive method for the production of cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs). Herein, a deep eutectic solvent (DES) system based on choline chloride (ChCl) and ethylene glycol (EG) was employed as the swollen solvent, combining with screw extrusion and permeant, to fabricate unmodified CNFs with high yield and thermal stability. The proposed method in this work was simple, convenient, and industrially viable. The hydrous DESs were applied in the process of CNFs preparation and dispersion to reduce the cost and viscosity of DES. To reveal the principle of CNFs preparation, the impact of sulfuric acid and water content of DES system on the chemical, physical, morphological, thermal, and dispersive properties of CNFs was systematically studied. Properties of the dispersed solvents were characterized by solvatochromic parameters and viscosity parameters to evaluate the potential influence on the preparation and dispersion of CNFs. In general, this work would play valuable guidance in realizing the preparation and dispersion of CNFs via a versatile DES solvent system, thus endowing cellulose materials high-value utilization. # 1. Introduction Cellulose, as an inexhaustible and widespread natural and green polymer (annual production capacity was around 75-100 billion tons worldwide), had attracted wide of increasing concern because of the global warming and depletion of petroleum sources [1,2]. Cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs), a kind of renewable and biodegradable cellulose nanomaterials [3,4], had received much attention in recent years because of the excellent features such as high strength and stiffness, high specific surface area, low density, biodegradability, and renewability. These advantages suggested that CNFs had great potential application prospect in composites to replace plastics [5,6], gel materials [7,8], catalysis [9,10], adsorption [11,12], electronics [13,14], and biomedical systems [15]. However, the structural complexity of components in natural cell walls limited the productivity of CNFs. Therefore, more efforts should be devoted to developing a highly efficient and eco-friendly method for CNFs preparation, which was conducive to reap the full potential value of cellulose nanomaterials in the future. Cellulose fibrils contained crystalline and amorphous regions and it could be delaminated to CNFs via mechanical and mechanochemical methods. It was well known that the structure of cellulose fibrils was complex and tightly-packed formed by hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces. Therefore, the mechanical treatment could defibrillate the fibers and transformed to CNFs as the mechanical energy exceeded the interfibrillar bond energy. Common methods for mechanical production of CNFs included high-pressure homogenization [16], ball milling [12], grinding [17] and so on. Scientists gradually recognized the problem and have found some new approaches to compensate for the shortcomings of single mechanical treatment for CNFs preparation. Chemical or biological pretreatment could swell cellulose fibers and partially disrupt the hydrogen bond network of cellulose fibrils, thus increasing the accessibility of cellulose fibrils [19]. That is, compared to single mechanical treatment, combining biochemical pretreatments with mechanical action could be conducive to reduce the energy consumption and improve the efficiency of fibrillation during the process of CNFs preparation. Thus far, various kinds of biochemical pretreatments have been used in CNFs preparation, such as acid hydrolysis, oxidation reaction, enzymatic hydrolysis, and so on. In the pretreatment of acid hydrolysis, the representative species mainly contained mineral acids (like sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, and phosphoric acid) and organic acids (like p-toluenesulfonic acid, oxalic acid, and maleic acid). It was well known that the acid hydrolysis could remove the amorphous of cellulose and partially disrupt the hydrogen bond network of cellulose fibrils, thus benefiting the liberation of CNFs via various mechanical treatments [20]. Oxidation reaction of cellulose mainly consisted of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl radical (TEMPO)-mediated oxidation and periodate-chlorite oxidation. Oxidation reaction could selectively oxidize the primary hydroxyl groups to weaken inter-fibrillar hydrogen bonds of cellulose, which would facilitate the extraction of CNFs [21]. However, the main obstacles during the process of CNFs preparation such as the harsh chemical consumption, corrosion of the equipment, and impacting environment still existed. The principle of enzymatic pretreatment on cellulose was similar to acid hydrolysis. However, enzymatic pretreatment was milder and more eco-friendly compared with acid hydrolysis or oxidation reaction [22]. Unfortunately, there were still some drawbacks in enzymatic pretreatment such as long reaction time, high operation cost, and so on. Therefore, to achieve the balance on economy and ecology, it is indispensable to explore a greener, simpler, and more inexpensive method for the pretreatment of cellulose. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), as new green solvents with biode- gradability and eco-friendly nature, were simply synthesized by mixing hydrogen-bond donors (HBD, such as quaternary ammonium salts) with hydrogen-bond acceptors (HBA, such as amines, amides, carboxylic acids, polyol) [23]. This meant that the properties of DESs could be flexibly designable through adjusting the HBA and HBD types and molar ratios to meet practical application needs. Apart from the above, DESS possessed many distinct physicochemical properties similar to ionic liquids, such as low melting points, negligible vapor pressure, high thermal stability, and nonflammability [24]. It was known that ionic liquids were recognized as good solvents for treatment of cellulose [25]. Thus, more and more researches employed DESs as the swollen solvents to pretreat the biomass to produce CNFs. Liu et al. applied an acidic DES based on choline chloride and citric acid in the pretreatment of bleached softwood kraft pulp and combined with high-pressure homogenize to prepare CNFs [26]. Hong et al. selected the DES composed of choline chloride and oxalic acid to swell the luffa sponge and adopted a two-step ultrasonication treatment to prepare elongated CNFs [27]. Unfortu- nately, DESs employed as swollen solvents in the process of CNFs preparation were commonly acidic DESs in most researches, which would cause the side reactions like esterification between acidic DESS and CNFs. More than this, it was known that high viscosity of DESs was a key problem, which would cause mass transfer problems and low dissolution mass concentration [28]. High cost of DESs was another key concern hindering the widespread application of DESs. Adding water to the DES system was recognized as a simple, efficient and low-cost method to tailor the properties of DESs, which could reduce the vis- cosity and cost of DESS [29]. To our knowledge, there were still few studies on the hydrated natural DESs applied in the preparation and dispersion of unmodified CNFs remained among the gaps. Herein, we aimed to use a natural DES as the swollen solvent fol- lowed by extrusion and permeation to prepare unmodified CNFs with high yield and thermal stability. The proposed method in this work was simple, convenient, and industrially viable. Moreover, to reduce the cost and viscosity of DES, the hydrous DESs were innovatively applied in the process of CNFs preparation and dispersion. Ethylene glycol (EG) was recognized as one of common biomass-derived polyols and showed a high boiling point and fascinating compatibility with biomass. In this work, EG was employed as HBD and choline chloride as HBA to syn- thesize the natural DES, which was used as a well-swollen solvent to pretreat cellulose under high temperature. Then, the swollen cellulose fibers were crushed and permeated using a screw extrusion device. After 423 M. Yan et al. International Journal of Biological Macromolecules 191 (2021) 422–431 a small quantity of sulfuric acid catalysis, the obtained samples in different dispersive solvents (DES, hydrous DESs, and aqueous phase) were further fibrillated by mechanical milling (Fig. 1). To reveal the principle of CNFs preparation and dispersion, the impact of sulfuric acid and water content on the chemical, physical, morphological, thermal, and dispersive properties of CNFs was systematically studied. Moreover, physicochemical properties (e.g., viscosity, acidity, basicity, and polarity) of DES were denoted using solvatochromic parameters including E_NR, Kamlet–Taft parameters (K-T parameters) (e.g., π*, α, and β) values [30,31], and viscosity parameters. Then, the potential relationships between these parameters of DES and the preparation of CNFs were evaluated. The results provided insights into chemical, physical, and structural changes of CNFs in response to varied quantities of sulfuric acid and water content of DES. This work would play valuable guidance in realizing the preparation and dispersion of CNFs using a DES solvent system. ## 2. Material and methods ### 2.1. Materials The Needle Bleached Kraft Pulp (NBKP) was provided from Jiangsu Province of China. Sulfuric acid (H2SO4, 98%), Ethylene glycol (C2H6O2, 98%), Choline chloride (C5H14ClNO, 98%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Bio-Chem Technology Co. Ltd., China. Cupri- ethylenediamine solution (C2H18N4O2Cu) was purchased from China National Pulp and Paper Research Institute. All chemicals were used as received without any purification. ## 2.2. Methods The uniform and clear DES was synthesized by ChCl and EG at a molar of 1:1 under 100 °C for 1 h. Four hydrated DESs were obtained by mixing the DES with water at the mass ratio of 80:20, 60:40, 40:60, and 20:80, which were referred to as 80% DES, 60% DES, 40% DES, and 20% DES, respectively. The NBKP of oven-dry weight was torn into small pieces and pretreated by DES at a mass ratio of 1:8 (120 °C, 120 min) with mechanical stirring for sufficiently swelling. After this procedure, the crushed cellulose (CC) was obtained using a screw extrusion device (CZR-2014, Guangzhou Chunziran Co. Ltd., China) 3 cycles under 100 °C. The type of screw extrusion was a single screw with L/D ratio of 20 and rotate speed of 55 rpm. 0%, 0.2%, 0.4%, 0.6%, and 0.8% w/w H2SO4 (based on the CC dispersion system) as a catalyst was separately dripped into the CC dispersion system, which was diluted to 5% solid content. The CC dispersion system was fully swelled at 100 °C for 0.5 h to insure that H2SO4 was permeated into the CC dispersion system. The obtained samples with the optimized H2SO4 amount were directly diluted to 0.8% concentration using DES, 80% DES, 60% DES, 40% DES, 20% DES, and distilled water (DW), respectively. Then the diluted samples were refined at 6000 rpm for 40 min under ambient temperature using a colloid mill with the narrow gap between the rotor and the stator was 0.1–3.0 mm (JIM-150, Wenzhou Kangding Machinery co. Ltd., China). Finally, before freeze-drying for later evaluation, the obtained different CNFs samples were dialyzed in DW for 7 days to completely remove DES. The obtained different CNFs samples were named as DES-CNF, 20% DES-CNF, 40% DES-CNF, 60% DES-CNF, 80% DES-CNF, and DW-CNF, respectively. ## 2.3. Characterizations The yield of CNFs was calculated from the equation as follow: Y(%) = w₁ / w₂ × 100% (1) where Y was defined as the yield of CNFs, W₁ was defined as the freeze- dried weight of. CNFs (after dialysis), and W2 was defined as the initial weight of raw material (oven dry). A JEOL-JEM 7600F scanning electron microscope (SEM) was employed to observe the morphologies of CNFs samples. CNFs samples were prepared from CNFs suspensions with a concentration of 0.01 wt% and deposited on a silicon wafer and air-dried. The distribution of fibril diameter was measured using ImageJ software. The degrees of polymerization (DPv) of raw material and CNFs were measured using an Ubbelohde viscometer based on the Mark-Houwink-Sakurada equation [32]. DPv^0.905 = 0.75[η] (2) The X-ray diffraction (XRD) of CNFs samples was measured by an X-ray refractometer (Ultima IV, Japan) with CuKa radiation (40 kV and 30 mA) in the range from 5° to 50° at a scan rate of 2°/min. The crystallinity degree (Cr) of CNFs samples was calculated based on the Segal method [33]: Cr = (I_002 - I_am) / I_002 x 100% (3) The Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) spectrogram of CNFs samples was made using a Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer (Vertex 80 V Bruker Germany) in a spectral range of 4000–450 cm⁻¹ with a resolution of 2 cm⁻¹. The thermogravimetric analyses (TGA) of NBKP and CNFs samples were conducted on a thermogravimetric analyzer (NETZSCH, TGA 209F1, Germany). CNFs Samples of 6-10 mg were evaluated from 30 °C to 600 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C/min under a 20 mL/min nitrogen stream. DES-CNF, 80% DES-CNF, 60% DES-CNF, 40% DES-CNF, 20% DES- CNF, and DW-CNF were dispersed in DES, 80% DES, 60% DES, 40% DES, 20% DES, and DW at a concentration of 0.1 wt% to observe the dispersion of CNFs samples, respectively. The obtained CNFs dispersions were sonicated in a bath sonicator (Avantech AC220, 600 W, 40 kHz) for 20 min and then evaluated their transmittance using a TU-1900 ultra- violet-visible spectrophotometer (UV-vis) in the range of the wave- length of visible light. The solvatochromic properties [31] of DES and hydrated DESs were characterized by solvatochromic parameters including E_NR and K-T parameters (π*, α, and β) values according to the method reported in the literature. E_NR was quantified the polarity of solvents and Kamlet–Taft parameters (K-T parameters) including α, β, and π* were quantified hydrogen-bond donating ability (acidity), hydrogen-bond accepting ability (basicity), and polarity/polarizability, respectively. The viscosity of DES and hydrated DESs were tested using a digital viscosimeter (FANGRUI, NDJ-001, China). All samples were measured by three replicates and the averages were reported. ## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. CNFs preparation The flowchart of CNFs preparation was schematically shown in Fig. 1. DESs, as emerging kinds of solvents synthesized by HBA and HBD, were much significant for the swelling of cellulose [34]. It was found that EG exhibited good compatibility with cellulose according to the previous literature [35]. Moreover, EG was one of the biomass-derived polyols and it possessed a high boiling point. Conclusions High-yield and thermostable CNFs were successfully prepared via DES based on ChCl: EG swelling, screw extrusion and permeant, a minimum supply of sulfuric acid catalysis and colloidal milling, while preserving the natural chemical structure of CNFs. The hydrous DESs were innovatively applied in the process of CNFs preparation and dispersion to reduce the cost and viscosity of DES. To reveal the principle of CNFs preparation and dispersion, the impact of sulfuric acid and water content on the chemical, physical, morphological, thermal, and dispersive properties of CNFs was systematically studied. Introduction Cellulose, as an inexhaustible and widespread natural and green polymer (annual production capacity was around 75-100 billion tons worldwide), had attracted wide of increasing concern because of the global warming and depletion of petroleum sources [1,2]. Scientists gradually recognized the problem and have found some new approaches to compensate for the shortcomings of single mechanical treatment for CNFs preparation. Chemical or biological pretreatment could swell cellulose fibers and partially disrupt the hydrogen bond network of cellulose fibrils, thus increasing the accessibility of cellulose fibrils [19]. That is, compared to single mechanical treatment, combining biochemical pretreatments with mechanical action could be conducive to reduce the energy consumption and improve the efficiency of fibrillation during the process of CNFs preparation. Thus far, various kinds of biochemical pretreatments have been used in CNFs preparation, such as acid hydrolysis, oxidation reaction, enzymatic hydrolysis, and so on. In the pretreatment of acid hydrolysis, the representative species mainly contained mineral acids (like sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, and phosphoric acid) and organic acids (like p-toluenesulfonic acid, oxalic acid, and maleic acid). It was well known that the acid hydrolysis could remove the amorphous of cellulose and partially disrupt the hydrogen bond network of cellulose fibrils, thus benefiting the liberation of CNFs via various mechanical treatments [20]. Oxidation reaction of cellulose mainly consisted of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl radical (TEMPO)-mediated oxidation and periodate-chlorite oxidation. Oxidation reaction could selectively oxidize the primary hydroxyl groups to weaken inter-fibrillar hydrogen bonds of cellulose, which would facilitate the extraction of CNFs [21]. However, the main obstacles during the process of CNFs preparation such as the harsh chemical consumption, corrosion of the equipment, and impacting environment still existed. The principle of enzymatic pretreatment on cellulose was similar to acid hydrolysis. However, enzymatic pretreatment was milder and more eco-friendly compared with acid hydrolysis or oxidation reaction [22]. Unfortunately, there were still some drawbacks in enzymatic pretreatment such as long reaction time, high operation cost, and so on. Therefore, to achieve the balance on economy and ecology, it is indispensable to explore a greener, simpler, and more inexpensive method for the pretreatment of cellulose. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), as new green solvents with biode- gradability and eco-friendly nature, were simply synthesized by mixing hydrogen-bond donors (HBD, such as quaternary ammonium salts) with hydrogen-bond acceptors (HBA, such as amines, amides, carboxylic acids, polyol) [23]. This meant that the properties of DESs could be flexibly designable through adjusting the HBA and HBD types and molar ratios to meet practical application needs. Apart from the above, DESS possessed many distinct physicochemical properties similar to ionic liquids, such as low melting points, negligible vapor pressure, high thermal stability, and nonflammability [24]. It was known that ionic liquids were recognized as good solvents for treatment of cellulose [25]. Thus, more and more researches employed DESs as the swollen solvents to pretreat the biomass to produce CNFs. Liu et al. applied an acidic DES based on choline chloride and citric acid in the pretreatment of bleached softwood kraft pulp and combined with high-pressure homogenize to prepare CNFs [26]. Hong et al. selected the DES composed of choline chloride and oxalic acid to swell the luffa sponge and adopted a two-step ultrasonication treatment to prepare elongated CNFs [27]. Unfortu- nately, DESs employed as swollen solvents in the process of CNFs preparation were commonly acidic DESs in most researches, which would cause the side reactions like esterification between acidic DESS and CNFs. More than this, it was known that high viscosity of DESs was a key problem, which would cause mass transfer problems and low dissolution mass concentration [28]. High cost of DESs was another key concern hindering the widespread application of DESs. Adding water to the DES system was recognized as a simple, efficient and low-cost method to tailor the properties of DESs, which could reduce the vis- cosity and cost of DESS [29]. To our knowledge, there were still few studies on the hydrated natural DESs applied in the preparation and dispersion of unmodified CNFs remained among the gaps. Herein, we aimed to use a natural DES as the swollen solvent fol- lowed by extrusion and permeation to prepare unmodified CNFs with high yield and thermal stability. The proposed method in this work was simple, convenient, and industrially viable. Moreover, to reduce the cost and viscosity of DES, the hydrous DESs were innovatively applied in the process of CNFs preparation and dispersion. Ethylene glycol (EG) was recognized as one of common biomass-derived polyols and showed a high boiling point and fascinating compatibility with biomass. In this work, EG was employed as HBD and choline chloride as HBA to syn- thesize the natural DES, which was used as a well-swollen solvent to pretreat cellulose under high temperature. Materials The Needle Bleached Kraft Pulp (NBKP) was provided from Jiangsu Province of China. Sulfuric acid (H2SO4, 98%), Ethylene glycol (C2H6O2, 98%), Choline chloride (C5H14ClNO, 98%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Bio-Chem Technology Co. Ltd., China. Methods The uniform and clear DES was synthesized by ChCl and EG at a molar of 1:1 under 100 °C for 1 h. Four hydrated DESs were obtained by mixing the DES with water at the mass ratio of 80:20, 60:40, 40:60, and 20:80, which were referred to as 80% DES, 60% DES, 40% DES, and 20% DES, respectively. The NBKP of oven-dry weight was torn into small pieces and pretreated by DES at a mass ratio of 1:8 (120 °C, 120 min) with mechanical stirring for sufficiently swelling. After this procedure, the crushed cellulose (CC) was obtained using a screw extrusion device (CZR-2014, Guangzhou Chunziran Co. Ltd., China) 3 cycles under 100 °C. The type of screw extrusion was a single screw with L/D ratio of 20 and rotate speed of 55 rpm. 0%, 0.2%, 0.4%, 0.6%, and 0.8% w/w H2SO4 (based on the CC dispersion system) as a catalyst was separately dripped into the CC dispersion system, which was diluted to 5% solid content. The CC dispersion system was fully swelled at 100 °C for 0.5 h to insure that H2SO4 was permeated into the CC dispersion system. The obtained samples with the optimized H2SO4 amount were directly diluted to 0.8% concentration using DES, 80% DES, 60% DES, 40% DES, 20% DES, and distilled water (DW), respectively. Conclusions High-yield and thermostable CNFs were successfully prepared via DES based on ChCl: EG swelling, screw extrusion and permeant, a minimum supply of sulfuric acid catalysis and colloidal milling, while preserving the natural chemical structure of CNFs. The hydrous DESs were innovatively applied in the process of CNFs preparation and dispersion to reduce the cost and viscosity of DES. To reveal the principle of CNFs preparation and dispersion, the impact of sulfuric acid and water content on the chemical, physical, morphological, thermal, and dispersive properties of CNFs was systematically studied. It was found that the properties of solvents (such as viscosity, solvatochromic properties) had a relationship with the preparation and dispersion of CNFs. More strikingly, the light transmittance of DES-CNF suspension was up to 72.2% and it could remain stable standing for 30 days, showing favorable dispersion and stability. In conclusion, this work, which was simple and industrially viable, would play valuable guidance on realizing the preparation and dispersion of CNFs via a versatile DES solvent system, thus making cellulose materials high-value utilization.
